blocks.x: COM SKILLS 157 · Communication Skills · Topic 1

Every sentence you speak or write in English is built from nine kinds of words, each behaving by its own rules. This topic gives you the vocabulary to identify each word class by its form, position and function — the same three-part lens KNUST examiners expect you to apply to any word in context.

9parts of speech in English: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, determiners and interjections 2broad categories — lexical (open class, carry meaning alone) and non-lexical (closed class, get meaning from context) 3lenses for identifying any word class: its form, its position, and its function in the sentence
By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Identify the various parts of speech in the English language — recognising each of the nine word classes when you meet them in a sentence.

2Explain the form, positions and functions of the various parts of speech in English sentences, using the correct grammatical terms (subject, object, complement, appositive, attributive, predicative, and so on).
3Use these parts of speech to form correct sentences in English, applying the rules of plural formation, possession, tense, comparison and word order that each class follows.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Lexical (open class) items Words that carry semantic content — they have meaning in themselves even when they stand alone. They are called "open class" because they readily accept new members (new nouns and verbs enter English all the time). The lexical items are nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.

Non-lexical (closed class) items Words that do not carry semantic content on their own — they get their meaning mainly from the lexical words around them in context. They are "closed class" because they do not accept new members. The non-lexical items are prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, determiners and interjections. Unlike lexical items, closed classes have no specific form — no particular suffixes or affixes identify them.

Form, position and function Form is the shape a word can take — how it is built up and the changes it can undergo (e.g. adding -s, -ed, -er). Position is the kind of words it occurs with, and where, in a sentence. Function is its usage or role in the sentence (e.g. subject, object, complement). A word's actual part of speech is only realised in context — it must take the right form, sit in the right position, and do the right job all at once.
Lexical vs. non-lexical at a glance
Nouns→ Verbs→ Adjectives→ Adverbs→ Prepositions→ Pronouns→ Determiners→ Conjunctions→ Interjections

items: The same word can belong to more than one word class depending on how it is used. Consider the word "chair" in the sentence "They chair the occasion." — here it is not a noun (a piece of furniture) but a verb, because it has verb form (bare form after "they"), verb position (after the subject, starting the predicate) and verb function (expressing an action).

The same test applies to a word like "up": it can be an adverb ("He looked up"), a noun/adjective-like predicate ("The time is up") or even a noun ("some ups and downs") — its class depends entirely on its form, position and function in that sentence.
This is why memorising a word in isolation is not enough for the exam — you must be able to justify its class from the sentence it appears in.

blocks.x: Lexical item 1 of 4

Nouns name the people, places and things a sentence is about. They are identifiable by characteristic suffixes, by the way they change to show number and possession, by where they sit in a phrase, and by the four jobs they can do in a sentence.
What is a noun?
Noun A word that names people, places or things. Nouns are one of the four lexical (open class) word classes, alongside verbs, adjectives and adverbs.
Identifying nouns by their suffixes
Words that end with certain suffixes are often identifiable as nouns:
-er
teacher, preacher, player, writer
-ion
nation, consultation, meditation
-or
doctor, pastor, mentor, actor
-ness
fitness, dryness, foolishness
-hood
womanhood, childhood, neighbourhood
Nouns and number: singular vs. plural

items: 1Most count nouns add "s". E.g. book → books, pen → pens, dog → dogs.
2Nouns ending in "y" after a consonant drop the "y" and add "ies". E.g. lady → ladies, country → countries, baby → babies, pantry → pantries.
3Nouns ending in "o", "ss", "sh", "ch" or "x" add "es". E.g. mango → mangoes, kiss → kisses, brush → brushes, church → churches, box → boxes. (Exceptions exist, e.g. photos, pianos.)
4Some non-count nouns keep the same form whether singular or plural, e.g. news, luggage, knowledge.

blocks.x: Nouns and possession

Possessive inflection
A noun showing possession indicates that it is the owner of a thing or person. The apostrophe rule depends on whether the noun is singular or plural, and whether it already ends in "s".

c: John's bag, James's bag (or James' bag)

blocks.x: Where nouns sit in a phrase

After determiners Most common nouns come after determiners (a, an, the, his, hers, etc.). Proper nouns do not normally take determiners, unless they are accompanied by a dependent clause that narrows them down. E.g. "She is the Ama I met yesterday."
Four functions of nouns in sentences
Nouns perform four main functions: subject, object, complement and appositive.

Noun as subject The subject comes before the main verb of the sentence. E.g. Kwame goes to school (Kwame = S, goes = V, to school = A). Based on the meaning conveyed, a noun functions as subject when it is:

items: 1the agent/performer of an action — e.g. Esi writes slowly.
2the possessor or recipient of an action — e.g. Kwasi has a car.
3a place — e.g. Rooms are always stuffy.
4a time — e.g. Yesterday was his birthday.
5an event — e.g. Parties are always lovely.

blocks.x: Other items can also function as subject: noun phrases (The woman in white is my mother.), noun clauses (The rumour that she travelled is true.) and pronouns (She is my mother.). Grammatically, the subject agrees in number and person with the main verb.

Noun as object Objects occur after transitive verbs. E.g. Kofi eats rice. Objects may be entities affected by the verb's action (The man beats his wife.), indicate location (Kofi climbed the mountain.), or be the result of the activity (Mummy prepared rice.).
Indirect object (IO)
Often comes before the direct object. E.g. Kofi gave Mary the book. (Mary = IO, the book = DO). It may instead be introduced by a preposition: Kofi gave the book to Mary.
Direct object (DO)
The entity directly receiving the verb's action. In Kofi gave the book to Mary, "the book" is the direct object and "to Mary" is a prepositional phrase carrying the indirect object.

Noun as complement Nouns (and noun phrases, noun clauses, adjectives or adjective phrases) can function as complements. A subject complement follows a copular/linking verb and describes the subject: My father is a farmer. An object complement directly follows and modifies the direct object: They consider their puppy their baby.

Noun as appositive A noun, pronoun, noun phrase or noun clause set beside another noun or pronoun to rename, explain or identify it. E.g. Nana Akufo-Addo, the President of Ghana, is a brave man. The appositive can also come first: The President of Ghana, Nana Akufo-Addo, is a brave man.

blocks.title: Quick self-check: which of the four functions?

items: "Rooms are always stuffy." → "Rooms" is the subject, designating a place.
"Kofi gave Mary the book." → "Mary" is the indirect object, "the book" is the direct object.
"My father is a farmer." → "a farmer" is a subject complement following the linking verb "is".
"Nana Akufo-Addo, the President of Ghana, is a brave man." → "the President of Ghana" is an appositive renaming "Nana Akufo-Addo".

blocks.x: Lexical item 2 of 4

Verbs are action words — but they also express states and processes. They change form to mark tense and aspect, sit in a predictable position after the subject, and split into several overlapping classification systems that KNUST exams test heavily: lexical vs. auxiliary, finite vs. non-finite, active vs. passive.
What is a verb?
Verb An action word — though, as covered below, verbs can also express states and processes, not just actions.
How verbs change to show tense
Tense The shape a verb takes to indicate distinctions in time.

items: 1Bare form — no structural change; used with first person singular/plural and third person plural subjects. E.g. I eat. / The woman and her son (they) eat.

2Simple present tense — formed by adding -s, -es or -ies, used with third person singular subjects. E.g. Esi / she carries the bag. It expresses present events, habitual events, universal truths, actions simultaneous with the present moment, and sometimes future or past time.
3Simple past tense — regular verbs add -d or -ed; irregular verbs change form entirely, e.g. come → came, sit → sat, run → ran.

4Aspect — verbs add -ing, -d or -ed together with a helping (auxiliary) verb to show whether an action is progressive or completed. E.g. She is going to school. (progressive) / She has gone to school. (completed)

blocks.x: Where verbs sit in a sentence
After the subject Verbs usually come after the subject of a sentence and begin the predicate, often in a declarative sentence. E.g. The chairman tabled the motion before the house.
What verbs express
States
He is a good man. / The woman looks beautiful.
Actions
She sweeps the compound every day.
Processes
Babies grow.
Lexical vs. auxiliary verbs
Lexical verb (main verb) Denotes the main action engaged in and does not require the presence of an auxiliary — it can exist alone in the sentence. E.g. She smiled.

Auxiliary verb (helping verb) A verb that helps another verb. There are two types: primary auxiliaries — all the forms of do, have and be (which can also act as ordinary action verbs on their own) — and modal auxiliaries — can/could, may/might, shall/should, need, will/would, dare, must, ought to and used to.
What auxiliaries help verbs express

items: 1Tense-aspect combinations — e.g. I am singing (present continuous), I was singing (past continuous), I have eaten (present perfect), I had eaten (past perfect).
2Mood — modal verbs change the grammatical mood of a sentence to express possibility (It might rain.), ability (It can rain.), necessity (It must rain.), or suggestion (It should rain.).
3Voice — whether the subject is the agent of the action (active voice: She ate the food.) or the target of the action (passive voice: The food was eaten by her.).

blocks.x: Finite vs. non-finite verbs
Finite verb
1. Marks/has tense (present or past). 2. Has a subject, with concord (agreement) between that subject and the verb. E.g. She reads a lot. / The men walk every morning.
Non-finite verb
1. Does not mark tense. 2. May not have a subject.
There are four classes of non-finite verb phrases in English:

c: to cook, to eat, to dance

items: "She smiled." → a lexical verb — it needs no auxiliary to stand.
"I have eaten." → "have" is a primary auxiliary marking present perfect aspect; "eaten" is the lexical verb in its past-participle (non-finite) form.
"It must rain." → "must" is a modal auxiliary expressing necessity.
"The food was eaten by her." → passive voice — the subject "the food" is the target, not the agent, of the action.
"She reads a lot." → a finite verb — it marks present tense and agrees with the subject "she".

sections.title: What is an adjective, and how is it formed?

blocks.x: Lexical items 3 & 4 of 4

Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe almost everything else — verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. Both classes share a family resemblance: characteristic suffixes, and comparative/superlative forms that let you compare two or more items.
What is an adjective, and how is it formed?
Adjective A word that describes a noun. Many adjectives can be identified by characteristic suffixes.
-ic
romantic
-ful
faithful
-al
logical
-ous
famous
-ive
attractive
Comparative & superlative degrees

-er / -est Many adjectives use the suffix -er for the comparative degree (comparing two items) and -est for the superlative degree (comparing three or more items). E.g. Esi is bigger than Ama. (comparative) / Esi is the biggest of them all. (superlative)
Positions that indicate function
Attributive position
Occurs between a determiner and a noun, modifying that noun phrase. E.g. A hardworking player was on their team.
Predicative position
Occurs in the predicate — following a linking verb (He is hardworking.) or after an object, in an SVOC pattern (My daughter made me proud.).

Postposed adjectives Adjectives that follow directly after the word they modify, e.g. heir apparent, court martial. Indefinite pronouns such as something, someone, anyone are also modified by postposed adjectives, e.g. something strange, anyone capable, someone good.
What is an adverb, and how is it formed?

Adverb A word that modifies verbs, adjectives or other adverbs, answering the questions how, where, why or when an action takes place. Like adjectives, some adverbs use -er/-est for comparative and superlative degrees, e.g. He is faster than you. / He is the fastest of them all. Many adverbs are also identifiable by the suffix -ly.
The mobility of adverbs

Mobility Adverbs can begin the sentence, end the sentence, or (in some cases) come immediately after the subject. E.g. Usually, we go on holidays. / We go on holidays usually. / We usually go on holidays. When an adverb is not properly placed it can cause ambiguity — the safest rule is to place the adverb next to the headword it is meant to modify.
Types of adverbs, by function
Adverb phrases can perform all of the same functions as single-word adverbs. These functions are what give rise to the types of adverbs:

items: 1Time — e.g. The alarm went off yesterday.
2Manner — e.g. Present your case carefully.
3Place — e.g. Here, the situation is different.
4Frequency — e.g. She comes here often.
5Reason — e.g. As it's Friday, you can stay up another hour.
Adjectives modify nouns only; they occupy attributive (before the noun), predicative (in the predicate) or postposed positions.
Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs; they are far more mobile and can appear at the start, middle or end of a sentence.
Both classes can take -er/-est to show comparative and superlative degrees.
Misplacing an adverb (unlike an adjective, which usually sits fixed next to its noun) is a common source of ambiguity in student writing.

sections.title: Linking nouns and phrases to the rest of the sentence

blocks.x: The five non-lexical word classes

These five closed-class items make up the "grammatical glue" of English — they don't carry meaning by themselves, they don't accept new members, and (unlike nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs) they have no specific identifying suffix. You know them only by their position and function.

Closed word classes have no specific form Unlike lexical items, the closed word classes — prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, determiners and interjections — have no particular suffixes or affixes that identify them. You must rely on position and function to recognise them.
Linking nouns and phrases to the rest of the sentence

Preposition A word that links nouns, pronouns and phrases to other words in a sentence. The word or phrase a preposition introduces is called its object. E.g. in "The book is leaning on the table," "the table" is the object of the preposition "on".

items: 1Position: prepositions normally precede their objects. Sometimes the preposition is separated from its complement (whatever completes/comes after it), e.g. "The man whom we gave the book to" instead of "The man to whom we gave the book."

2Prepositional phrases are built the same way — a preposition followed by a complement (also called the object of the preposition), which may be a pronoun, a noun phrase, or a gerund (a verb in its -ing form). E.g. I bought a bag for him (prep + pronoun); The cat is under the table (prep + noun phrase).

blocks.x: Types of prepositions and their uses
Time: at, on, in
at for specific times — The bus will leave at 4:00am tomorrow. on for days/dates — My father is coming on Monday. in for non-specific times of day, month, season or year — He started the job in 1982.
Place: at, on, in

at for specific addresses — The ceremony will be held at Bomso L/A Primary. on for streets/avenues — Her house is on Ridge Road. in for land-areas (towns, countries, continents) — She lives in Kumasi.
Movement: to
to expresses movement towards a place — They were walking to school together. Toward/towards are also useful for expressing movement.
Anaphoric elements that replace nouns
Pronoun An anaphoric element used to replace a noun. E.g. The lady opened the refrigerator. She opened it. — "she" replaces "the lady" and "it" replaces "the refrigerator".

Position: pronouns can occur as subjects (She is happy.) or as objects (Kofi gave the book to me.). Function: pronouns identify nouns, show possession, designate places, and more — the specific functions depend on the type of pronoun.
Personal, demonstrative & interrogative pronouns

Personal pronouns Refer to specific people or things and change form to indicate person, number, gender and case. English has three persons: first person — I (singular), we (plural), e.g. I am happy.; second person — you (singular or plural), e.g. You are my friend.; third person — he, she, it (singular) and they (plural), e.g. She is a lecturer. They were writing.
Demonstrative pronouns Point to and identify a noun or pronoun: this, that, these, those. E.g. This tastes good. That phone is mine. Those are my friends. These cakes are delicious.

Interrogative pronouns Introduce questions — the wh-words: what, which, who, whom, when, whose. "Who" and "whom" refer to people; "which" and "what" refer to things or animals. E.g. What did he say to you? Who asked the question? What is that? Who will buy me a pen? Which do you prefer?

Reading assignment: relative pronouns, indefinite pronouns, reflexive pronouns and intensive pronouns are also part of this topic — review these types alongside personal, demonstrative and interrogative pronouns.
The little words that precede and modify nouns

Determiner "Those little words that precede and modify nouns" (Afreh, 2006). Examples: the, a, that, a bit of. Determiners precede nouns and noun phrases, and are always followed by a noun — they are said to "mark" nouns.

items: 1Specify nouns — e.g. The cat is mine.
2Show possession — e.g. That was hers.
3Show quantity — e.g. How many books are they?

blocks.x: Joining grammatical units together
Conjunction A word used to join similar grammatical units — words and words, phrases and phrases, or clauses and clauses. Examples: but, or, while, before, yet, and, so.

items: 1Join words, phrases and clauses — e.g. The boy and the girl (phrase and noun); The girl is good but the boy is naughty (clause and clause).
2Show contrast between two grammatical units — e.g. conjunctions like but and yet.
3Indicate subordination in clauses — e.g. because, while, if, since.

blocks.x: Expressing strong emotion or excitement

Interjection A word (or group of words) used to express strong emotions or excitement. Because they express strong emotion, interjections are usually identified in sentences with an exclamation mark. Examples: ouch!, hey!, shhh! Position: like adverbs, interjections are very mobile — their position in a sentence can change.

items: 1Demand or request something, usually forcefully.
2Express emotions like disgust.
3Greetings — e.g. Hello!
4Mark hesitation — e.g. Errm!
5Express surprise — e.g. Wow!
"The cat is under the table." → "under" is a preposition; "the table" is its object.
"Kofi gave the book to me." → "me" is a pronoun functioning as object.
"The cat is mine." → "The" is a determiner specifying "cat".
"The girl is good but the boy is naughty." → "but" is a conjunction joining two clauses and showing contrast.
"Wow! That's a big fish." → "Wow!" is an interjection expressing surprise.
